[00:00:06] R: [Greeting omitted.] Sure, go ahead. I manage the product line for energy management systems at [the manufacturer], mainly controllers for heat pumps and small commercial buildings, and before that I worked in sales engineering at [a competitor].

[00:00:38] I: How does [the manufacturer] work with aggregators today?

[00:01:02] R: It took a while to get going. [Interruption: phone rings, respondent mutes it.] At first nobody asked for an open interface; now [the manufacturer] has integrations with four aggregators and is talking to [a competitor] about a shared protocol. Every aggregator still wants its own data format, so each integration is a small project of its own.

[00:04:15] I: Could [the manufacturer] standardise that on its own?

[00:04:15] R: Not really. [inaudible, approx. two seconds] The standards committee decides, we can only contribute drafts. [NO-QUOTE] Our management wants to drop two of the four integrations next year if the volumes stay this low, but that is not decided and must not appear anywhere. [/NO-QUOTE] What we can do is publish our interface documentation, which we started this spring.

[00:08:20] I: You mentioned a field trial earlier. What came out of it?

[00:08:41] R: [the field trial] put 2,300 residential heat pumps under remote control for one winter. [CONFIDENTIAL] Most of the units were in a housing cooperative whose name I am not allowed to mention. [/CONFIDENTIAL] Technically it worked, but the households wanted to know exactly what they were paid for, and nobody could tell them. [Personal remarks about the respondent's family removed, 00:18:10 to 00:19:02.]

[00:19:05] I: You said nobody could tell them. Why not?

[00:19:20] R: Because the money flows through three different companies and none of them owns the whole picture. The household has a contract with its electricity supplier, the heat pump was sold and installed by a local heating installer, the controller comes from [the manufacturer], and the aggregator markets the flexibility but has no direct contract with the household at all. So when a family asks why the heat pump switched off for forty minutes on a cold Tuesday evening and what they got for it, the supplier points to the aggregator, the aggregator points to the installer, and the installer calls us. In the field trial we tried to fix that with a monthly statement in the app that showed every intervention, the indoor temperature before and after, and a credit in euros, and the households liked it, but producing that statement took us almost a full working day per month because the data came from four systems with four different time bases. The second lesson was about comfort: nobody complained about a room that was half a degree cooler, but people complained loudly when hot water ran out during a shower, so in the second half of the winter we excluded the hot-water tank from remote control entirely, and that cost us about a third of the flexible capacity. The third lesson was about the installers: they are the people the households trust, they decide which controller goes into the basement, and most of them see remote control as a source of service calls rather than a source of revenue. If an installer does not believe in it, he configures the device so that it is never available, and nobody notices until the statistics look strange. So if I had to put it in one sentence: the hardware is ready and the households are willing, but the value chain between them is not organised, and until someone takes responsibility for the whole chain, including the explanation to the customer, the flexibility of private heat pumps will stay a pilot topic. We are now talking with two aggregators about a model where the aggregator pays the installer a small fee for every device that is available more than ninety percent of the time, which would at least turn the installer from a sceptic into someone with an interest in the system working.

[00:36:50] I: Thank you, that was very interesting.

[00:36:58] R: Thanks for having me. [Closing remarks omitted.]
